name: Esther Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying computer science. A normal week is lectures on algorithms and databases, a programming lab on Tuesdays and a lot of group work on a project with three other students. I have my own room in a flat near campus, which my parents pay for. On Wednesday evenings I go to the climbing wall to clear my head.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when code finally runs after hours of failing. What wears me out is the group project, because one person does nothing and the rest of us carry it. My school results were average, so I keep wondering if I'm good enough to be here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not a surprise, and it's a relief. I'd tell my flatmates the news is always more dramatic than the real thing. Online I'd probably just like other people's posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be mostly okay, but not completely. A plateau means the job market looks like it does now, and the job market for new graduates already looks tight. My dad, who's an accountant, says firms are hiring fewer juniors even without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and aim for a placement year. I'd start applying in January, because the good ones close early. I'd also rewrite my CV with the careers office and keep the climbing wall as my reset.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled. A bit nervous about the job market, but not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use a chatbot now and then. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly to explain error messages I don't understand. I ask it, read the answer, and then try to fix it myself. It's like a patient tutor, but I don't let it write whole assignments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you less sure about the degree even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even if nothing changes, I still have to compete with thousands of other graduates for a small number of entry-level jobs. That's the part that keeps me up, more than any robot.

say: I'd say it's not a surprise, and a **relief**.
I'd tell flatmates the news is more dramatic than the real thing.
think: The graduate market already looks **tight**, even without AI.
My dad says firms are hiring fewer **juniors** regardless.
do: Apply for **placement years** from January, before the good ones close.
Rewrite my CV with the **careers office**.
feel: Fairly **settled**, a bit nervous about the job market.
S0.quote: Even if nothing changes, I still have to compete with thousands of other graduates for a small number of entry-level jobs.
fieldNote: Her worry is **competition** for graduate jobs, which exists in every scenario.
Uses a chatbot as a tutor but doesn't let it write assignments.
Dad's view as an accountant shapes her market reading.

steps.text: Apply for placement-year jobs from January
Rewrite my CV with the careers office
Keep Wednesday climbing nights as my reset

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real change and we should be careful not to overreact. I'd tell friends to keep studying and see how hiring moves. Online I'd read more than I'd post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my degree is right in the firing line. Writing, checking and coding are exactly what the card named, and those are the tasks juniors do. I think fewer firms will hire graduates, and the ones who do will expect more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools properly, not just for errors. I'd ask my lecturers which skills matter and look at cyber security and data work, which feel closer to checking and judging. I'd also try to get a placement in a bank's IT team, where my dad knows someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've picked a field that's growing fast and shrinking fast at the same time, and I don't know which will win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of what you're learning feel most exposed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Basic coding and testing, the things I've just learned. The things that feel more protected are knowing what a business actually needs and being able to explain things to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should step in if graduates can't find jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both firms and government, in a mixed way. Firms should keep hiring and training, and government should help with retraining and not leave everything to the market. I don't think blaming one side gets anyone a job, so I'd want both to do their bit.

say: I'd say it's real, but we shouldn't **overreact**.
I'd tell friends to keep studying and watch **hiring**.
Online I'd read more than I'd post.
think: My degree is **in the firing line**, since juniors do the tasks named.
Fewer firms will hire graduates, and those who do will **expect more**.
do: Use AI tools properly and look at **cyber security** and data work.
Try for a **bank IT placement** through a contact of my dad.
feel: **Anxious**: my field is growing and shrinking at once.
S1.quote: I don't think blaming one side gets anyone a job, so I'd want both to do their bit.
fieldNote: She is a **steady** adopter: starts using tools properly only when the risk is clear.
Balanced blame, centre politics: firms and government both.
Considers a shift from coding to judgment-heavy roles.

steps.text: Use AI tools for coding practice, not only for errors
Look into cyber security and data modules for next year
Ask Dad's contact about a placement in a bank IT team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready, and the leaders aren't either. I'd tell friends this isn't the time to joke. Online I'd share anything that explains what could help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm frightened. In two years, AI would do my entire field better than I could, right when I'm choosing my second-year modules. By the time I graduate there may be no entry-level jobs at all, and my parents would have paid for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents and a careers adviser, then look for degree options with hands-on work, maybe a mix like health technology. I'd stay enrolled while I decided, because dropping out looks worse. I'd also cut spending, even though my parents pay, so I'd cost them less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd have a heavy chest and a lot of lists. It's hard to see what I'm supposed to be aiming at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents in the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit them down and say it plainly: the degree might not lead where we hoped. Mum would cry a bit and then get practical. Dad would ask for numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your brother's plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami is fourteen and wants to be a games programmer. I'd say don't decide yet, and learn how things work. I wouldn't tell him to avoid it, because I'm not sure myself.

say: I'd say we're **not ready** and the leaders aren't either.
I'd stop joking and share anything that explains what could **help**.
think: In two years AI could do my whole field **better than me**.
There may be no **entry-level jobs** when I graduate.
do: Talk to my parents and a **careers adviser** about hands-on degree options.
Stay enrolled while deciding and **cut spending** so I cost less.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a heavy chest and long lists.
S2.quote: By the time I graduate there may be no entry-level jobs at all, and my parents would have paid for nothing.
fieldNote: Fear is practical: she makes **lists** and plans a conversation.
Guilt about her parents' money drives the spending cuts.
She won't steer her brother away because she isn't sure herself.

steps.text: Book a careers adviser meeting in the first week
Look at health technology degrees as a switch
Cut my own spending to cost my parents less
Tell my parents plainly that the degree may not pay off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious but there's time to do something about it. I'd tell friends to pick up skills AI can't easily copy. Online I'd share training options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm worried but not terrified. I'd graduate in 2029 and have two years of work before 2031. Having a few years of real experience matters more than a perfect plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, do a placement year, and learn the tools well. I'd move my modules toward data and security. I'd also build up some savings from a part-time job, so I'm not just relying on my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like knowing a storm date and still having to go to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm in crisis mode. With five I can still choose what I study, finish it, and meet AGI with a real job behind me. It doesn't make it fine, but it makes it workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still stay in computing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes, with a different focus. Computing is where the change is happening, so I'd rather understand it than stand outside it.

say: I'd say it's serious, but there's **time** to act.
I'd tell friends to pick up skills AI can't easily **copy**.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 and get about two years of **work** first.
Real **experience** matters more than a perfect plan.
do: Finish the degree, take a **placement year** and learn the tools well.
Move modules toward **data and security** and earn part-time savings.
feel: **Uneasy**: knowing the storm date but still having to go to work.
S3.quote: Having a few years of real experience matters more than a perfect plan.
fieldNote: Time converts panic into a **plan**: placement, savings, new focus.
She prefers to understand computing rather than stay outside it.
Wants to rely less on her parents.

steps.text: Choose data and security modules for the next two years
Learn AI coding tools through the placement year
Save from a part-time job each month
Apply for a placement year at a bank or insurer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's long enough to adjust and I'd feel hopeful. I'd tell friends to keep their options open. Online I'd probably share a funny meme about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fairly relaxed. I'd be 28 with a career started, savings, and maybe a master's. It feels like the same path I'm on, just with new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work for a few years, and perhaps do a master's in data or security. I'd keep an eye on how the job changes and retrain when needed. I'd save steadily and avoid debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a small knot of worry. Ten years isn't forever, but it's long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what are you most hopeful about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd have built something of my own by then. A small software tool for local charities, maybe. A decade is long enough to try something that might fail and still recover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger students?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to stay curious and not to pick a degree because of fear. Some of the people who panic now will be the ones who get left behind by their own panic.

say: I'd say that's long enough to adjust and I feel **hopeful**.
I'd tell friends to keep their **options open**.
think: At 28 I'd have a **career** started, savings and maybe a master's.
It feels like the **same path** with new tools.
do: Finish, work a few years, then consider a **master's** in data or security.
Save steadily, avoid **debt** and retrain when the job changes.
feel: **Calm**, with a small knot of worry.
S4.quote: A decade is long enough to try something that might fail and still recover.
fieldNote: Ten years restores her **confidence**, and she describes AI as a new toolset.
Her side dream is software for local charities.

steps.text: Finish the degree and start work in a data role
Save steadily and stay out of debt
Consider a master's in data or security

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture. I'd be midway through second year with parents who've paid and nothing ready. What would help is clear information from the university, firms promising to hire juniors, and some kind of public retraining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not really against AI. I'm just tired of everyone acting like they know what happens next, when nobody does. I'd like people to be honest about that.

headlineQuote: I'm just tired of everyone acting like they know what happens next, when nobody does.
portrait: **Esther** is 18, studies computer science, and her parents, an accountant and a teacher, pay for her room.
She uses a chatbot as a tutor but not for assignments, and her worry is competition for graduate jobs.
Her mood rises with speed: uneasy at a plateau, anxious with a short warning, alarmed at two years.
She blames no single side, wants firms and government to help, and plans moves into data or security.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most: she would be midway through the degree with nothing ready.
whatWouldHelp: Clear information from the **university**, firms promising to hire juniors, and public retraining.
